The liver is the star: a transplanted piece can grow to the right size for the child within weeks to months, much like a pruned plant filling its pot. A transplanted adult kidney doesn’t keep growing with the child in the same way; it may get a bit bigger, but it mainly works so well from the start that the child “grows into” it. Hearts and lungs don’t regenerate new parts after transplant; they can enlarge to a degree as the child grows, often enough to meet the body’s needs, but they don’t expand the way a liver does. In short: livers truly grow, kidneys are usually already powerful enough, and hearts/lungs need closer size matching up front.

“Not responding” usually means the program’s front desk has stopped picking up the phone. Desktop apps have a main “event loop” that does two simple jobs: it reads a stream of messages from the operating system (things like “the mouse clicked here,” “redraw this button,” “the window was moved”) and it answers them. Imagine a mailbox at the app’s door that fills with letters from you and the system. As long as someone keeps opening envelopes and acting on them, the app feels alive. If that person stops—no clicks are handled, no screen updates are painted—the mailbox overflows, and after a short timeout the operating system slaps on the label “Not Responding.” The computer isn’t frozen; that program’s receptionist just isn’t answering.

Why does the receptionist stop? Commonly, the program is busy doing a long task on that same front-desk thread: crunching numbers, loading a giant file, or talking to the network in a way that waits and blocks. Sometimes it’s stuck at a red light waiting for a resource—like holding one key and waiting for another key that a different part of the program is also holding (a deadlock). Other times it’s running in circles (an endless loop), or the system is shuffling memory back and forth so much that progress crawls. While this happens, your clicks and “please repaint” requests pile up unheard, so buttons don’t depress and windows don’t refresh. The fix on the developer’s side is to keep the front desk free: move heavy work to background helpers, break big jobs into small chunks that periodically return to the event loop, use non-blocking (asynchronous) operations, and be careful with locks. As a user, your choices are to wait and hope the backlog clears, or force the program to close if it never comes up for air.

A black hole is what you get when a lump of stuff collapses inside its own “no-escape” boundary, in a universe that is otherwise just sitting there. That picture quietly assumes there’s an “outside” region you could, in principle, escape to. The Big Bang wasn’t a lump exploding into empty space; it was space itself stretching everywhere at once. There was no outside to escape to, and no stationary background to collapse against. From the very first moments, the fabric of space was expanding extremely fast, so gravity could at most slow that expansion, not instantly reverse it into one giant collapse.

Think of it like this: a black hole is a local cave-in; the Big Bang is the entire ground rising. You can have a cave-in in a field, but you can’t have “the whole field cave in” if the field is what defines “down” in the first place. On top of that, early space was astonishingly smooth—ripples in density were only about one part in 100,000, as we see in the cosmic microwave background. Black holes need a sizable bump in density so gravity can overwhelm pressure and expansion in that spot. Because the early universe lacked big bumps, it didn’t turn into one super–black hole. At most, rare over-dense patches could have collapsed into small “primordial” black holes—an idea still under investigation—while the rest kept on swelling like raisin bread in the oven.

Think of space as a very slowly stretching rubber sheet with coins lying on it. The stretching tries to pull the coins apart. But many coins are tied together with strong rubber bands. The sheet can stretch all it wants; coins that are banded together don’t drift apart. In the universe, the “sheet” is space itself expanding, while the “rubber bands” are the forces that bind things: gravity for galaxies and solar systems, and electromagnetism for atoms, molecules, and rocks. Expansion increases the distance between far‑apart, unbound regions of space; it doesn’t pry apart things that are already held together.

On human and even galactic scales, the stretch is incredibly feeble compared with those binding forces. Your body, the Earth–Moon system, the solar system, and even the Milky Way are glued together so firmly that the gentle pull of cosmic expansion is utterly drowned out. Only on the largest scales—between galaxies that are not gravitationally bound, and especially between clusters of galaxies—does the stretching show up clearly as they drift away from each other over billions of years.

What about energy? Light traveling through expanding space gets its wavelength stretched, shifting to redder colors; in that sense, radiation “expands” with the universe. Matter does not puff up; it just gets more spread out on average because there’s more space between clumps. In our current universe, the expansion is too mild to tear apart bound structures, and there’s no need to worry about atoms or solar systems being pulled to pieces by it.

No. Prime numbers never run out. A prime is a whole number greater than 1 that is divisible only by 1 and itself. Over 2,000 years ago, Euclid gave a timeless proof: suppose you listed every prime that exists, multiplied them all together, and then added 1. This new number can’t be evenly divided by any prime on your list—it always leaves a remainder of 1—so either it’s a new prime or it has a prime factor you didn’t list. Either way, your “complete” list wasn’t complete. So there must be infinitely many primes. Think of the number line as a long coastline with lighthouses (the primes) placed at irregular intervals; they may spread out, but there is no final lighthouse.

It’s true the gaps between primes can grow. In fact, you can make a very long stretch with no primes at all: multiply all the numbers from 2 up to some n, then add 2, 3, 4, …, n; each of those results is divisible by one of the numbers you multiplied, so they’re all composite. That builds a man‑made “desert” of consecutive non‑primes as long as you like. Yet beyond any such desert, an oasis appears: another prime. So while primes get rarer as you travel farther, there is no point on the number line after which they cease to exist.

“Species” is a label we use to mark branches on the family tree of life. It isn’t a magic line; it’s more like a fence we put up when a branch has grown on its own long enough to be clearly different. Neanderthals and modern humans are two sister branches that split from a common ancestor roughly 600,000 years ago. Think of a river forking: each channel flows through different terrain, shaping its own banks. Over time, those separate paths left consistent, diagnosable differences.

Neanderthals had a distinct build and skull shape—long, low crania with heavy brows, big noses, and a stockier body adapted to cold climates—while modern humans have rounder skulls and more gracile bodies. Their genomes also form a separate cluster: Neanderthals share about 99.7% of their DNA with us (very close, but consistently distinct), and their lineage carried unique genetic variants. Crucially, they lived mostly in Ice Age Europe and western Asia while early Homo sapiens evolved mainly in Africa, so their breeding pools were largely separate for hundreds of thousands of years.

But didn’t they interbreed? Yes—when the two rivers briefly rejoined, some water mixed. Many people today of European or Asian ancestry carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA. That shows compatibility, but limited mixing didn’t erase the long, independent histories or the clear anatomical and genetic differences. Because of that sustained separateness and diagnosable traits, most researchers classify Neanderthals as a different species (Homo neanderthalensis). A minority prefer calling them a subspecies of Homo sapiens, and the debate reminds us that “species” is a human tool for describing nature’s messy edges, not a rigid rulebook.

Think of a single hair as a very fine cable wrapped in overlapping roof shingles. Those “shingles” (the cuticle) are made of keratin, a protein dotted with water‑loving spots. Water molecules are tiny and slightly charged, so they stick to these spots through gentle electrical attractions (like weak magnets). Some water slips under the shingles and into the inner core, making the hair fiber swell a little—more like a sponge than a piece of plastic. That’s why wet hair feels heavier and takes time to dry: you’re not just wiping the surface; you’re waiting for water to leave the inside, too.

Now zoom out to a whole head of hair—a dense forest of fibers. Between neighboring hairs are narrow gaps that act like tiny straws, pulling and holding water by capillary action, the same way dew clings between blades of grass. The roughness of each hair and the overlapping scales trap thin films and droplets, and when strands touch, little water bridges form that are surprisingly stubborn. Damaged or “porous” hair, with lifted or chipped shingles, hangs on to even more water; smoother hair (or hair coated with conditioner oils) holds less because water can’t grip as well and slides off more easily.

Put simply: hair holds water well for three reasons—its chemistry (protein that likes water), its structure (a scaly surface over a sponge‑like interior), and its crowd behavior (many fibers creating water‑trapping gaps). Heat and moving air help because they break those weak attractions and sweep moisture away, turning a wet forest back into a dry one.

Short answer: your lungs don’t have a wash cycle, and there’s no scrub brush or “detox” that removes tobacco tar on command. But they do come with a cleanup crew. Tiny moving hairs (cilia) sweep mucus upward like airport conveyor belts, and immune cells act like janitors picking up debris. When you stop smoking, those cilia start working again within weeks, mucus clears better, inflammation drops, and over months to years a lot of the particles are gradually carried out. That said, some “soot” stays stored in lung tissue and nearby lymph nodes for life, and structural damage—like emphysema or scarring—is more like knocked-down walls than spilled coffee: it doesn’t rebuild.

What helps most is simple and powerful: stop smoking completely and avoid secondhand smoke so the cleanup crew can do its job. There’s no proven lung cleanse; time, clean air, hydration, regular physical activity, and, if needed, pulmonary rehabilitation improve how well the lungs move air and clear mucus. Vaccinations and prompt treatment of infections prevent setbacks. As the lungs recover, health risks steadily fall—heart attack and stroke risk drops within a year, and lung cancer risk declines over the next decade—though some risk remains above that of a never-smoker. Think of quitting as closing the chimney; the room airs out, the dust gets swept, but the faint stain on the bricks is a reminder—one that fades, but doesn’t fully vanish.

Short answer: the core experience is more alike than different. In both men and women, orgasm is a short, whole‑body reflex controlled by the nervous system. As arousal peaks, the brain flips into a brief “electrical storm,” heart rate and breathing jump, pelvic floor muscles fire in rhythmic pulses, and the brain releases feel‑good chemicals like dopamine, oxytocin, and endorphins. Picture two different instruments playing the same musical crescendo: the notes (the reflex and brain chemistry) are remarkably similar.

The main differences are in the packaging. In most men, orgasm is tightly linked to ejaculation and is usually followed by a longer “refractory period,” a downtime before another climax is possible. In many women, there’s no ejaculation link and the refractory period is shorter or absent, so multiple orgasms can happen more easily, and the pattern can feel more variable from one occasion to another. People also differ widely in what kind of stimulation brings them there—though anatomically, much of the female response routes through the clitoral network, whether the sensation feels external or internal. Big picture: same basic wiring and storm, but the weather forecast—how long it lasts, how many waves, how quickly it returns—varies more from person to person than it does between sexes.

Short answer: insects almost certainly have the bug-equivalent of an itch, even if it isn’t the same private feeling you and I have.

Think of an insect’s body as a fur coat made of tiny antenna-like hairs. Each hair is wired to nerves that notice the slightest touch, speck of dust, drop of liquid, or hitchhiking parasite. When those sensors fire, they trigger very specific cleaning routines: flies rub their forelegs like they’re lathering up, then sweep their eyes and antennae; they cross their legs like little brooms to comb debris off; bees and ants pick and brush at spots where mites or spores land, and even help each other “groom.” In lab tests, sprinkling fine powder on a fly makes it home in on that exact body part and scrub until it’s clear—much like you scratch the one place that tingles.

What we can’t say is whether a fly “feels itchy” the way a human does; insects can’t report feelings, and their brains are simpler. But they have the same functional loop: a local “something’s on me” signal that drives a targeted scratch-or-clean action until the signal stops. So while a mosquito may not brood about an itch, its nervous system still rings the tiny alarm and sends it to the nearest built‑in brush.

Short answer: no. Think of the atmosphere as a bathtub, emissions as the tap filling it, and forests as a sponge that can soak up some water. The number 638 GtC is how much carbon is already stored in all forests (the size of the sponge), while 9.8 GtC is how much we pour into the tub each year (the flow from the tap). Carbon‑neutrality compares annual flows: to be neutral, the sponge must soak up as much each year as we pour in each year. Increasing forest carbon by 1.5% would add roughly one year’s worth of extra storage in total, not every year. And that extra storage would accumulate slowly over decades as trees grow, not instantly.

Real‑world details make the gap bigger. New forests don’t absorb carbon at a constant high rate forever; they start slowly, peak during mid‑growth, then level off as they mature. Some of the added carbon can be lost again through fire, pests, or logging, so it isn’t guaranteed permanent. Converting other lands to forest can also release soil carbon at first, and suitable land, water, and nutrients are limited. In practice, forests are essential allies—protecting and restoring them can remove meaningful amounts of carbon over time—but they complement, not replace, deep cuts in fossil‑fuel emissions. To get to carbon‑neutral, we need both: rapidly turn down the tap and help the sponge keep soaking.

Think of a spider starting a web the way engineers span a canyon: first send a feather-light line across, then use it to build something stronger. An orb-weaving spider climbs to the top of one pole, stands on tiptoe with its abdomen raised, and lets out a very fine silk thread from tiny nozzles at its rear. A small breeze (and even faint electric forces in the air) carries this gossamer like an invisible kite string. When the drifting end brushes the opposite pole, it snags on the rough surface. The spider gently tugs to test it. If it slips, the spider reels the line back in and tries again; if it holds, the spider anchors its end firmly and sets the first “bridge.”

With a bridge in place, the spider walks across, adding a second strand as it goes to strengthen and tighten the line. Now it has its own “overhead support.” From the middle of this bridge, it drops down to form a triangle, then builds a sturdy frame around the edges. Next come the spokes running to the center, and finally the sticky spiral that actually catches insects. So even between two bare poles, the spider doesn’t need something above—it manufactures the first connection by mailing a silk thread across on the wind, then turns that single line into an entire web.

On land, your eye focuses mostly with the clear front window, the cornea. Think of it as a curved windshield that bends incoming light so it lands sharply on the retina, the “film” at the back of the eye. The cornea works so well because air is on one side and eye tissue is on the other; that air-to-eye boundary makes light bend a lot. Underwater, the outside is water, which bends light almost the same way the cornea does. The windshield stops shaping the beam, and the eye’s focus falls behind the retina, so everything looks blurry—like wearing the wrong prescription. A dive mask fixes this by putting a thin pocket of air back in front of the cornea.

Aquatic animals solve this by carrying their own powerful “magnifying glass” inside the eye. Fish have very round, strong lenses and relatively flat corneas, so the lens—not the cornea—does almost all the bending of light. They focus by sliding that lens forward and backward, like moving a camera lens along a rail. Marine mammals that split time between water and air (seals, sea lions, dolphins) use big, very flexible lenses and strong focusing muscles, letting them reshape focus across both worlds. The trade‑off is that some are razor‑sharp underwater but a bit nearsighted in air unless they actively refocus.

Water itself is a dim, blue-green room: it scatters light and quickly eats warm colors like red and orange. To cope, many aquatic eyes have wide pupils, retinas packed with light-hungry rods, and even a mirror-like layer behind the retina that bounces unused light back for a second chance, boosting sensitivity. Put together, these changes let underwater animals see clearly and brightly where our eyes, built for air, quickly give up.

Think of your USB drive as a notebook the computer borrows. “Eject” means: finish writing, close the notebook, and put the elastic band around it. If you just pull it out, you might be yanking the notebook away while the computer is still scribbling or while it’s holding some notes in its head (memory) to write later. If that happens, the latest changes can vanish, files can be saved only half-finished, and the drive’s table of contents (the map of where everything is) can get muddled—leading to errors the next time you plug it in.

Often, nothing bad appears to happen, especially if no files were open and no copies were in progress—modern systems try to reduce the risk. But the chance of silent damage is real. The safe routine is simple: wait for any copy progress to finish, close any files you opened from the drive, click Eject (or Safely Remove), and wait for the confirmation or for the drive’s light to stop blinking. If you absolutely must unplug in a pinch, do it only when the drive looks idle, and be ready to run a repair tool and keep good backups. The hardware itself is usually fine; it’s your data and the drive’s “map” that are at risk.
